paper.title: Architectural Features for Artificial Intelligence & Blockchain in the Nano-Era
paper.abstract: Artificial Intelligence and Blockchain are among the most computationally demanding domains. They request tremendously powerful computation engines capable to deliver fast, cheap and energy aware solutions. Here we present the functional aspects and the structural and architectural requirements best suited for implementing the technological environment which allows an emerging safe & intelligent world. Finally, we assert the improvements required from the emerging nano-technologies, focused mainly on the interconnection problems raised by the current implementations of big cellular one-chip systems.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Architectural requirements for AI and blockchain workloads, answered by the authors' previously published Map-Scan-Reduce many-cell accelerator (Connex lineage), with requests to nano-technology.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** The proposed structure is described as "already described in few versions in [14] [15] [20] [21]"; the paper motivates and re-describes an existing architecture rather than contributing a new algorithm or proof. Asymptotic statements (O(log n) loop latency, O(n) size) are asserted, not derived.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (no numbered definitions)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: ~15 predicated vector/instruction semantics (e.g. `WHERE(cond): bi <= bi & condi ? 1 : 0`, `REDADD: acc <= sum(bi ? acci : 0)`), plus vector notations Vi, B, IX, ACC.

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate — the conditional-assignment expressions specify instruction semantics of the accelerator in the register-transfer style hardware architects use; a programmer or hardware designer implementing the instruction set would need exactly this. Borderline items are the bracket notations for vectors (`IX = [1 2 ... n]`, `S =< s1 s1 ... sn >`, the latter with a typo), which are plain-English-expressible but are notational shorthand rather than set-theoretic decoration. No necessity-test failure recorded.

### Issues
The sequence `S =< s1 s1 . . . sn >` repeats s1 (typo). The DELETE semantics refer to an undefined index `p`.

---

## Citation Analysis

Self-citations: 7/24 (29%): [14] Maliţa, Popescu, Ştefan; [15] Maliţa, Ştefan, Thiébaut; [18] Ştefan, Maliţa; [19] Ştefan; [20] Ştefan, Maliţa; [21] Ştefan et al.; [22] Ştefan, Mihai. [16] (Mîţu and Mîţu) is not by the authors. All self-citations concern the Connex/Map-Scan-Reduce line or (for [22]) consensus via IT, which the paper links to blockchain voting; relevance is acceptable (>= 0.5 for most, [22] marginal). Many references are web pages, vendor material and a YouTube talk ([21]).

---

## Structural Analysis

The evaluation section is brief: "validated by three versions implemented in silicon" without data, a 28 nm estimate (2048 cells, 12 W), and a single SHA256 figure (46.8 MH/s/W, "3.37x" an Nvidia chip) compared against a consumer GPU review page [23]. State-of-the-art utilization figures are cited. Much of Section 2 is quotation from [17]. The claim-evidence balance is weak. Limitations are acknowledged inline in Section 6 (von Neumann bottleneck, latency trade-offs, algorithms whose scan/reduce latency cannot be hidden). No code, RTL, or data is released or linked.

---

## Conclusion

A perspective paper restating the authors' accelerator architecture against AI and blockchain workloads. The notation is functional rather than decorative, so no formalism flag is raised. Weaknesses are the thin, largely unsubstantiated evaluation, heavy quotation, web-heavy references, and a 29% self-citation ratio.

paper.title: New steps for advancing the Nothing On Insulator Triode 3nm gap and preliminary expanded technology
paper.abstract: This paper presents new steps of the Nothing On Insulator (NOI) device advancing. From the simulations point of view, a better swing is accomplished by shorter vacuum gap and the transistor replacement by triode. The actual simulated NOI-Triode with 3nm gap possesses lower swing versus the previous NOI-Triode of 14nm gap. Functional simulations prove the current density vectors from Source to Drain with substantial Gate leakage current. Comparisons with similar vacuum nanotransistors of other authors reveal similar ID-VDS and ID-VGS curves, with superior currents for the actual NOI-Triode 3nm gap. A preliminary technology, based on laser ablation by MALDI technique, produced a gap of 10µm in ABS-conductor micro-wires deposited on glass substrate. An accurate NOI architecture was accomplished, but at expanded sizes, defined by the laser spot resolution.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.EXCESSIVE_SELF_CITATION: 10 of 23 references (43%) are by the authors, nine of them with C. Ravariu: [6], [7], [8], [9], [13], [14], [19], [21], [22], [23]. Most are on NOI devices; [22] and [23] (organic nanocomposites, Fe3O4/PABA organic TFT) are only marginally related, supporting the gate-insulator and MALDI process steps.

verdict.summary: Incremental TCAD simulation study of a 3 nm-gap NOI vacuum triode plus a 10 µm laser-ablation prototype; formalism is minimal and appropriate, but self-citation is excessive (43%).

paper.title: Wideband Sub-terahertz Coplanar Waveguide-Fed Spiral Antenna
paper.abstract: This paper presents the design, simulation and characterization results of a wideband sub-terahertz membrane supported coplanar waveguide fed Archimedean spiral antenna. A fully parameterized 3D electromagnetic model was developed and a parametric study up to 350 GHz is performed. A 2 turns antenna placed over a metalized plate is optimized and the simulated results show |S11| < -10 dB between 60 - 150 GHz, a directivity of 7-10 dBi and a simulated efficiency larger than 60% between 70 - 150 GHz. The measured results showed good matching from 75 - 110 GHz, in good agreement with simulations, a measured antenna gain of 10.6 dBi at 94 GHz and a broadside axial ratio smaller than 3 dB between 77 - 97 GHz. With an compact membrane area of 5.3x5.3mm2 the performances of the proposed antenna are beyond the previously reported CPW fed spiral antennas.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.NO_LIMITATIONS: No limitations section or substantive inline acknowledgment; the only caveat is that the frequency-bound formulas are "only a first order approximation". The gain derived from measured 3 dB beamwidth and the measurement band restricted to W-band are not discussed as limitations.

verdict.summary: Solid design-simulate-fabricate-measure antenna paper with textbook equations used appropriately and low self-citation; lacks a discussion of limitations.

paper.title: Low cost approaches for High Resolution Digitally Programmable Potentiometers
paper.abstract: This paper aims to find adequate solutions for implementing a high resolution digitally programmable potentiometer by taking into consideration the production cost and also the performance indicators such as the linearity characteristics, wiper resistance and total resistance variations. All described solutions were implemented in a 5V 0.18µm CMOS process and their performances were verified by simulations.

paper.title: New Extraction Method of the Bipolar Transistor Model Parameters Used in Bandgap Voltage References
paper.abstract: A new extraction method of the critical model parameters affecting temperature variation of the bandgap type voltage reference is presented. According to the new method, the two model parameters describing the linear and non-linear temperature dependence of the bandgap type voltage references are extracted from the raw data of the reference voltage vs. temperature and not from direct measurements of the bipolar transistor.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.EXCESSIVE_SELF_CITATION: 5 of 14 reference entries (36%) are by the authors: [9], [10], [12], [13], [14], all S. Marinca patents or a paper with M. Bodea. [9] and [10] are identical entries (the same two US patents listed twice), inflating the count. All are on the bandgap/PTAT topic.

verdict.summary: Analytical two-temperature method for extracting VG0 and XTI from bandgap reference output, with derivations that are necessary and an error section; claimed accuracy gains rest on sensitivity arithmetic rather than validated measurements, and self-citation is excessive.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Extracting bipolar transistor parameters VG0 and XTI from a first-order-compensated bandgap reference's output at two temperatures, instead of from three-temperature Vbe measurements.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** The method is a short algebraic manipulation of the classical Vbe(T) expression; it is a simple refinement of existing extraction methods, without a new model or proof.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 30 (Vbe(T) model, three-point solutions, error expressions, bandgap balance, extraction formulas)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate — every equation is a working step of the derivation or extraction procedure that an engineer would implement. Many equations, but none decorative.

### Issues
Equation (20) writes the logarithm term as ln(kT/q), dimensionally inconsistent with the T/T0 form used elsewhere, suggesting a transcription error. Equation (11) writes "Vb e" and the section 6.3 heading reads "narrowingn".

---

## Citation Analysis

Self-citations: 5/14 (36%). [9] and [10] are the same pair of Marinca patents listed twice. [13] and [14] are further Marinca patents; [12] is a Marinca/Bodea conference paper. All are topically related, so no irrelevant-self-citation flag, but the ratio exceeds 30% and the duplicate entry is a citation-hygiene concern. Reference [4] lacks venue and year.

---

## Structural Analysis

The central claim, errors "smaller with more than one order of magnitude" than existing methods, is supported only by evaluating the authors' sensitivity expression (29) for a 0.1 °C error, not by comparison with independently measured parameters. Silicon results (16 LDO samples, Figs. 9-10) show distributions of extracted VG0 and XTI without a ground truth. A dedicated "Errors" section discusses PTAT nonlinearity, collector-current temperature dependence and bandgap narrowing, and defers "a more detailed error analysis" to future work. No data released.

---

## Conclusion

A practical, engineer-oriented extraction method with formalism that is entirely functional. Evidence for the claimed accuracy improvement is analytic rather than experimental, and 36% self-citation (with a duplicated self-cited entry) triggers the excessive self-citation flag.

paper.title: Analysis and design of a high efficiency current mode buck converter with I2C controlled output voltage
paper.abstract: This paper presents the analysis and design of a two-version current mode buck converter whose output voltage is set by a digital potentiometer programmed through an inter-integrated-circuit interface (I2C). The first version of this converter is an asynchronous rectifier variant (arv) while the second version uses synchronous rectification (srv). First version can handle up to 300W output power, having an input voltage of 48V and the output voltage ranging from 1.5V up to 40V with a maximum output current of 7.5A while the second version can handle up to 360W with a maximum output current of 15A. This converter uses a high voltage, high efficiency, fixed frequency controller with programmable soft start, undervoltage lockout, current limit unaffected by duty cycle and internal high voltage regulator for its gate driver. This current mode control (CMC) buck converter was designed to be integrated in a computer-controlled unit for electronic devices characterization (CCUEDC) as an upgrade of the internal hysteretic buck converter. It can be also integrated in a highly efficient and versatile lab power supply or to be used to power LEDs devices.

paper.title: A comparison between the Gm based implementations of voltage mode and current mode capacitance multipliers
paper.abstract: A comparison between two Gm based implementations of capacitance multipliers, one following a voltage mode perspective and another one following a current mode perspective is performed. The transconductor based circuit solution for voltage mode capacitance multiplication employs the Miller effect around a voltage amplifier implemented as a transconductance amplifier paired with another transconductor acting as a load. The current mode multiplier used as reference in the comparison uses the same components and is built around a typical current mirror by substituting the MOS transistors with transconductance amplifiers. For both structures the ratio of the two transconductances defines the multiplication factor. Due to the transconductance tunability, the multiplication factor is adjustable in a wide range. The results show an important advantage of the voltage mode multiplier with regards to the low frequency behavior in comparison to a current mode Gm-based implementation, recommending the voltage mode circuit for frequency compensation applications. A first order low-pass filter is implemented as an application of the two described architectures using discrete Gm integrated circuits.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Deriving and comparing input-impedance models of Gm-based voltage-mode (Miller) and current-mode capacitance multipliers, with 0.18 µm simulation and LM13700 board measurements via a first-order LPF.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** Standard small-signal analysis of known topologies and an empirical comparison.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 57 (nodal equations, impedance derivations, equivalent-circuit parameters, LPF measurement model)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate — the equations are the circuit analysis that yields the equivalent models (Ceq, Req, parasitic branches) on which the comparison rests; none fail the necessity test, though the ideal and non-ideal derivations partly duplicate each other.

### Issues
None in formalism. Editorial defects: Fig. 4's caption ("Linear polarization: (a) vertical (V) and horizontal (H); (b) slant (S) polarization") belongs to an antenna paper; Section 3 ends mid-sentence ("to implement the \"G\""); a paragraph in Section 6 is duplicated verbatim; Section 5's text says the current-mode multiplication factor denominator is smaller than the voltage-mode one written as gm2 + go1 + go2, inconsistent with the earlier go = go1 // go2 notation.

---

## Citation Analysis

Self-citations: 2/5 (40%). Both self-citations are the direct precursors of the two circuits compared, so topical relevance is high, but with only five references the paper engages minimally with the capacitance-multiplier literature and the self-citation ratio exceeds 30%.

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims are backed by analysis, simulation (Figs. 12-13) and measurements (Figs. 17-24); the stated agreement between theory and measurement is plausible. The measured low-frequency gain difference cited (-6.03 dB vs -6.05 dB) is small, and Figs. 23-24 show a selected subset of points (the authors disclose this selection). Limitations are acknowledged inline: poorer dynamic range and limited voltage swing of the voltage-mode multiplier. No design files or measurement data are released.

---

## Conclusion

Technically sound comparative circuit study with necessary formalism and real measurements. Editing errors (a caption from another paper, a truncated sentence, a duplicated paragraph) and a five-reference bibliography with 40% self-citation are the main concerns; the latter triggers the excessive self-citation flag.
